name: Jūnihon-yasu
age_estimate: several hundred years, often cited as roughly 800

location.address: Kiraichi, Aisonoyama, Kanagi-machi, Goshogawara, Aomori Prefecture, Japan (嗜良市字相野山)

access: Free, no permission needed. A forest road (Kiraichi-gawa Heiyo forest road) leads to a torii gate marking the sacred site, then a short walk to the tree. About 20 minutes by car from Kanagi Station; ja.wikipedia notes the forest road can close in winter due to snow.
transport: Kanagi Station (Tsugaru Railway) + approx. 20 minutes by car/taxi; no public transit reaches the tree directly
verify_notes: A Hiba (Thujopsis dolabrata / Hinoki-asunaro) that forks into 12 major branches about 4m up the trunk, resembling a fish-spear (yasu), which gives the tree its name. Local legend: a youth named Yashichiro who slew a demon monkey, and villagers planted a hiba sapling in memorial; also a belief that whenever a 13th branch sprouts one of the twelve always dies back, keeping the count at twelve. Around 1912-13 loggers were sent to fell it but the workers refused, and it was preserved instead (aomori-tourism.com). Selected for the 'Shin Nihon Meiboku Hyakusen' (New Japan's 100 Famous Trees), 1990. Designated a Goshogawara City natural monument, continuing the former Kanagi Town designation; a 2003 survey considered it for national Natural Monument status but this was not pursued because landowner consent for the site was not obtained (ja.wikipedia). AGE CONFLICT, not resolved: ja.wikipedia quotes a 2008 Goshogawara city council record verbatim, '樹齢は約800年、幹回りは約8メートル、樹高は約34メートルを測る' (age approx. 800 years, girth approx. 8m, height approx. 34m); a separate tourism blog (aomori-tourism.com) instead gives a wider 'estimated 300 to 800 years'. Girth used here (800cm) is the specific council-record figure; height 34m agrees across both sources. Location is confirmed from a geotagged Commons photograph (File:Junihonyasu_kiraichi_kanagi_goshogawara_aomori_japan.jpg, lat 40.9174882/lon 140.5137034) matching the given candidate coordinates almost exactly; a second, older Commons photo (File:Juunihon Yasu.jpg) carries a different, less precise geotag ~1.5km away and looks like an approximate placement, disregarded in favour of the two matching precise tags. SINGLE-FAMOUS-TREE TEST (would somebody travel specifically for this tree?): UNCLEAR, flagging honestly rather than deciding it myself. In favour: a distinctive, one-of-a-kind branching shape with its own legend, a national top-100 famous-tree listing, and multiple independent Japanese blog/trip reports (aomoritanken.com, ameblo.jp x2, t-ate.com) from people who drove out specifically to see it, which is the behaviour pattern of a destination tree among Japan's giant-tree ('kyoju') enthusiast community. Against: no English-language coverage found beyond monumentaltrees.com and Commons/Wikidata scaffolding, it sits down a forest road with no town or other attraction nearby, and its national Natural Monument bid was dropped, suggesting it is a respected local/enthusiast destination rather than a broadly famous one. Recommend treating as a lead pending Hidde's or a later pass's judgement on whether the destination bar is cleared, rather than shipping it alone as a place.
monumentaltrees_note: monumentaltrees.com/en/jpn/tohoku/aomori/3173_kanagimachi/ covers this tree (girth 7.30m at 1.30m height per its listing, visible only via WebSearch summary) but the page itself returned HTTP 403 to both curl and WebFetch and could not be read directly, so per the search-summary-is-a-lead-never-a-source rule its figure was NOT used as a source; recorded here only as a lead for a future pass with different network access.

name: Nago no Hinpun Gajumaru
access: Free, no permission needed. Stands beside a public road/small plaza in central Nago near the Anada Bridge over the Saichi River, flanked by Route 84; visible and reachable at any time.
transport: About 85 minutes by car from Naha Airport via the Okinawa Expressway (Naha I.C. to Kita I.C.); central Nago also has local bus service, but no train (Okinawa's only rail is the Naha monorail, which does not reach Nago)
verify_notes: A giant gajumaru (banyan, Ficus sp.) standing in the middle of Nago city, one of Okinawa's best-known individual trees and a designated symbol of Nago City. 'Hinpun' refers to the traditional Okinawan screen wall placed between a house's gate and its main building; the name comes from the 'Sanpu Ryumyaku-hi' stone monument at the tree's base, also called the 'Hinpun-ishi' (screen stone), erected in 1750 by the Ryukyuan statesman and feng-shui scholar Sai On. The tree was already well known enough to be mentioned in Ryukyuan Ryuka poetry by the 1690s. It originally grew beside a large pine, which it gradually enveloped; a 2002 typhoon damaged it and a 2010 conservation prune removed roughly 940kg of branches. DESIGNATION: Okinawa Prefecture natural monument since 19 October 1956, elevated to a NATIONAL Natural Monument (kunishitei tennen kinenbutsu) on 2 September 1997 -- one of Japan's official highest-tier heritage-tree designations, confirmed independently by both ja.wikipedia and the Ministry of the Environment's own giant-tree database (kyoju.biodic.go.jp), which lists it under Nago, Daito 1-chome, 1. FIGURES DISAGREE SLIGHTLY between the two sources, recorded rather than picked: ja.wikipedia gives height 19m, crown spread 30m diameter, and calls the trunk circumference itself 'unknown, obscured by aerial roots' while giving the aerial-root mass circumference as approx. 10m and age as '240 years or more' / 'over 300 years' (inconsistent within the same article); the Ministry of Environment database gives height 17m, girth 1180cm at breast height, and age 'estimated at 320 years'. Girth of 1180cm used here is the Ministry figure; note for the writer that a banyan's 'trunk' at breast height is a fused mass of aerial roots rather than a single stem, so this number describes that mass, not a single trunk as with most other species. SINGLE-FAMOUS-TREE TEST: PASSES clearly. This is a National Natural Monument, the acknowledged symbol of Nago City, has its own English-language Tripadvisor attraction page with visitor reviews, is covered by multiple English-language Okinawa tourism sites (okinawaclip.com, tokyocreative.com) independent of any city page, and stands alone in central Nago with no other published Ancient Trees entry within a day trip. This is the strongest single-tree destination candidate of the four in this batch.

name: Nomanji no Sotetsu

location.address: Nomanji Temple, 2517-1 Kataoka, Yoshida-cho, Haibara-gun, Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan

access: Free entry to the temple grounds; the Shizuoka Prefecture cultural-property record states the temple is open daily 9:00 to 17:00 with parking available. This is a working Buddhist temple, not a garden with a ticket booth, but its designated Natural Monument is a stated visitor draw and the prefecture's own record confirms regular public opening hours.
transport: Kataoka is in Yoshida-cho, Haibara-gun, central Shizuoka Prefecture; nearest station is JR Kikugawa or Fujieda on the Tokaido Line, then a short taxi/drive (no direct train to the temple).
verify_notes: IMPORTANT NAME CORRECTION: the brief's candidate name 'Nomanji' romanizes as 能満寺 (No-man-ji), not 野間寺 (Noma-ji) as the brief's transliteration guess suggested; Wikidata confirms the temple's kanji and gives the English label 'Nomanji no Sotetsu' matching Wikidata Q11611985. A Cycas revoluta Thunb. (identified as a male plant by the 1924 designation document), one of the 'Three Great Cycads of Japan' (alongside the Myokokuji cycad in Osaka and the Ryugenji cycad in Shimizu Ward, Shizuoka). DESIGNATION: national Natural Monument since 9 December 1924 (Taisho 13), one of the earliest tree designations under Japan's 1919 historic-sites/scenic-beauty/natural-monuments law, per the Shizuoka Prefecture cultural-properties database, which is the official designation record; the town of Yoshida's own tourism page independently corroborates the tree, its temple and its 1000-year local age tradition. LEGEND (recorded as legend, not fact): planted around the year 1000 by Abe no Seimei, the famous Heian-era onmyoji (yin-yang diviner), who is said to have sealed a serpent spirit beneath it; when Tokugawa Ieyasu later had it transplanted to Sumpu Castle it reportedly 'wept' for its old home every night until he had it returned. It is listed among the 'Enshu Nanafushigi' (Seven Wonders of Enshu) folklore set. FIGURES: the prefecture's 1924 designation text is in pre-metric units, quoted verbatim: '本樹ハ根廻リ一丈一尺數本ノ太キ枝ヲ分ツ其中ノ最大ナルモノゝ基部ノ周圍八尺四寸ナリ' (the plant's ROOT/BASE circumference is 1 jo 1 shaku, roughly 333cm, and it divides into several thick branches, the largest of which has a base circumference of 8 shaku 4 sun, roughly 254cm). girth_cm here (333) is that whole-clump root/base figure, converted from shaku/sun (1 shaku = 30.3cm); flag for the writer that this is a MULTI-STEMMED CLUMP of roughly 90 branches rather than a single trunk, so neither figure should be repeated as an ordinary trunk measurement. Height (approx. 6m) and branch count (approx. 90) come from Yoshida Town's own page and match figures repeated by several travel sites (rurubu.jp, jalan.net) that this pass did not need to fetch directly since two official sources already agreed. AGE FLAGGED: 'roughly 1,000 years' is temple tradition tied to the Abe no Seimei legend and is not an independently measured or scientifically dated figure (ja.wikipedia's own article notes no verification method); recorded as a broad, honestly-labelled estimate rather than a precise fact. SINGLE-FAMOUS-TREE TEST: reasonably PASSES. A national Natural Monument since 1924 (an unusually early and prestigious designation), one of Japan's culturally recognised 'Three Great Cycads', with its own Wikidata entry, an English Wikidata label, a Commons category, and a Tripadvisor attraction page for the temple (page itself 403'd to this pass's fetchers, but its existence is evidence of independent English-language tourist recognition). Less internationally documented than the Nago banyan, so flagging with slightly lower confidence than that one, but the national 1924 designation and the Three-Great-Cycads status are real, checkable claims of fame rather than local puffery.

name: Jakushin-san no Kusu
species: Camphor Tree (Camphora officinarum, syn. Cinnamomum camphora)

location.address: 618 Kitazako-machi, Kita Ward, Kumamoto City, Kumamoto Prefecture, Japan (Jakushin Ryokuchi park)

access: Free, no permission needed. The tree stands in Jakushin Ryokuchi, a public green space/park created around it in 1989 (formerly surrounding farmland); open ground, walk in freely.
transport: About 20 minutes on foot from JR Ueki Station on the JR Kagoshima Main Line
verify_notes: 'San' in the name is an honorific for a PERSON, not 'mountain': the tree is named for Kanokogi Chikakazu, a Sengoku-period retainer of the Kikuchi clan and lord of Kumamoto's precursor Kumamoto (Kumamoto/Chihaya) Castle, who took the Buddhist name Jakushin; tradition holds his grave sits at the tree's base, wrapped into its roots, hence 'Mr. Jakushin's camphor'. Every year on 11 January, the anniversary of his death, residents of the local Kitazako district gather under the tree for a Shinto rite marking the start of the new year, per the Japanese-language sources. One of Kumamoto Prefecture's largest camphor trees, with a distinctive above-ground root system whose shapes locals liken to animals and objects, making it a minor 'power spot'. Selected for the 'Shin Nihon Meiboku Hyakusen' (New Japan's 100 Famous Trees), the same 1990 national list as gsg_001 (Junihon-yasu) in this batch. DESIGNATION, from the Ministry of Environment's own giant-tree database (kyoju.biodic.go.jp): a Kumamoto Prefecture-designated Natural Monument since 1974. NOTE for the writer/future pass: a second official-adjacent source, the national Cultural Agency's own film-location database (jl-db.nfaj.go.jp), instead calls it 'a Special Natural Monument of Kumamoto Prefecture' in its English rendering; 'Special Natural Monument' (tokubetsu tennen kinenbutsu) is normally a much rarer NATIONAL tier reserved for a handful of Japan's most important sites, so this looks like an imprecise English translation of the ordinary prefectural designation rather than a genuinely higher tier, but it was not resolved against the original Japanese text of that source and is flagged rather than silently corrected. Damage from a 1991 typhoon broke many branches; the tree recovered. It declined again around 2010 from soil compaction by a nearby road, and recovered again after 2016 remediation (soil removal/treatment), confirming it is alive and actively maintained as of recent years. FIGURES: kyoju.biodic.go.jp gives girth 1710cm and height 30m; an earlier Japanese-language tourism search summary (not independently fetched, so not used as a source per the search-summary rule) had quoted a lower girth of 13.3m and height of 29m for the same tree, which is close enough to read as a rounding/measurement-year difference rather than a true conflict, but is noted here in case a future pass finds the original page it came from. Location confirmed from a geotagged Commons photo (File:寂心さんの樟 - panoramio.jpg) matching the candidate coordinates almost exactly. SINGLE-FAMOUS-TREE TEST: UNCLEAR, flagging honestly. In favour: an exceptionally large trunk (1710cm girth is enormous even among Japan's giant camphors), a purpose-built public park around it since 1989, an active annual community ritual, and a national top-100 famous-tree listing. Against: the designation is prefectural rather than national (unlike nag_001 and yos_001 in this batch), and this pass found no English-language tourism coverage beyond a government film-location directory entry; Kumamoto and Kyushu generally have many large camphors (Kamo no Okusu, Takeo's giant camphor, etc.) competing for the same 'famous camphor tree in Kyushu' attention, which weakens the case that this SPECIFIC tree is what draws the trip rather than being one of several similar options. Recommend treating as a lead pending further judgement rather than shipping alone.
